transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess the main thing is… I’m having a really hard time keeping my mind on things long enough to actually finish them. I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but it’s been getting in the way.

At work, for example, I’ll be trying to track down a client’s network issue, reading through logs, and then ten minutes later I realize I’ve gone over the same few entries three times and I still couldn’t tell you what they said. Even when it’s important, my attention just kind of slips off. That’s… basically why I’m here, if that makes sense.
Did you have problems paying attention when you were a child?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I don’t want to overstate it, but my mother still kind of jokes about my grade school report cards. They’d say things like I was bright, but I didn’t stay in my seat, or I’d blurt out answers. And apparently I lost homework even when I’d actually done it.

So… yes, I guess it was there back then too, if that’s the kind of thing you mean.
Do you have the same trouble focusing outside of work too?

Yeah… I think so. It’s not only work, though that’s where I notice it most because there are consequences.

Even at home, if I’m trying to finish something that needs steady attention, my mind just kind of wanders off before I get through it. I’ll reread the same thing or sit there meaning to keep going, and then realize I haven’t really taken any of it in. I don’t mean I’m not trying — I am — it just doesn’t seem to hold for very long. Does that answer what you mean?
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

Um… I don’t think so, not really. I mean, I get frustrated with myself, sure, but I wouldn’t say I’ve been feeling depressed. At least not in the way I understand it.

I’m not sure if that’s the kind of thing you’re asking, though.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to deal with?

I’m not sure I’d say I worry a lot, no. I mean, I think about things I need to handle, and sometimes I get stuck on whether I’m forgetting something, but I don’t know if that counts as worry exactly.

I wouldn’t want to make it sound bigger than it is. I guess I haven’t noticed myself worrying when there’s nothing going on. Is that what you mean?
Did these attention problems start after a particular stressful event or major change in your life?

I guess… not exactly after a stressful event in the sense of one single thing happening and then it started overnight.

But it did get seriously worse after I was fired. That was about… a year and ten months ago. I lost the routines and systems that were kind of keeping me on track, and since then it’s been much harder to manage. I don’t want to overstate it, but that’s when it became a real problem.
Before you were fired, were these attention problems causing significant trouble in your day-to-day life?

Before that… I mean, I had my ways of keeping things together, so I don’t know if I’d call it significant trouble then. Maybe some issues, but it was manageable.

The serious trouble really started after I was fired, about a year and ten months ago, when I lost the routines and systems that had been keeping me on track. Since then it’s been much harder day to day. Does that answer what you’re asking?
When your life feels more structured or stable again, do your attention problems mostly go back to how they were before you were fired?

Somewhat, yes… structure definitely helps. I don’t want to make it sound like I’m completely helpless without it, but when I don’t have something like the old ticketing system and escalation calendar, things kind of scatter.

My day turns into sticky notes, half-finished emails, chess club reminders, parts orders… and then I honestly have trouble telling what needs to happen first until something is already overdue. So if things are stable and structured again, I do better, but I’m not sure it goes all the way back to “fine,” if that makes sense.
After you were fired, did you feel so distressed by it that you had trouble coping with daily life?

I’m not sure I’d put it as “so distressed I couldn’t cope,” exactly. I mean, it was upsetting and embarrassing, definitely, and I didn’t handle it perfectly.

But I don’t know… daily life didn’t fall apart because of the feelings alone, if that’s what you mean. It was more that after it happened, I didn’t have the usual structure around me. Does that distinction make sense?
